title: Neonatal Seizures
sources: Critical Vector — Neonatology Pocket Guide: Neonatal Seizures
Pressler RM et al. ILAE Neonatal Seizure Task Force classification. Epilepsia 2021;62(3):615-628

changelog.change: Initial entry — jitteriness vs seizure, Volpe types, the etiology list (correct metabolic causes first), and the treatment ladder (phenobarbital → fosphenytoin / levetiracetam → pyridoxine trial).

purpose: Most neonatal seizures are subtle or focal (generalised tonic-clonic is rare — immature cortex). Correct glucose, calcium, and magnesium first, in parallel with an antiseizure drug if seizures are ongoing. Confirm with EEG / aEEG where available — clinical suspicion is unreliable in both directions.

rows: Eye movements
Normal
May be abnormal — staring, blinking, tonic deviation
Response to gentle restraint
Stops when the limb is held / flexed
Continues despite restraint
Movement quality
Fine, rhythmic tremor
Coarser; may have autonomic change (apnoea, tachycardia, BP swings)

items: Subtle — most common overall: ocular movements, oral-buccal-lingual (chewing / sucking), cycling limb movements, apnoea with tachycardia. Often NOT time-locked to EEG.
Clonic (focal / multifocal) — rhythmic jerking of one limb or one side; more often EEG-correlated than subtle.
Tonic (focal / generalised) — sustained posturing; focal tonic more often EEG-correlated.
Myoclonic — brief jerks; generalised myoclonus can be a poor prognostic sign and overlaps with severe encephalopathy.

body.text: Electro-clinical dissociation is well documented in neonates: some visible events have no EEG correlate (brainstem release phenomena), and many electrographic seizures have no clinical sign — especially after an antiseizure drug is given. Continuous EEG / aEEG is the reference standard; treat confirmed electrographic seizures even without a visible correlate.

rows: Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy
Most common overall; onset in the first 24 h after a perinatal hypoxic event; frequent but brief seizures
Intracranial haemorrhage
Term: subarachnoid after traumatic / macrosomic delivery, usually good prognosis. Preterm: IVH after day 3, generalised tonic, worse prognosis
CNS infection
Meningitis / encephalitis — consider if well at birth then deteriorates, or seizures beyond the first few days
Acute metabolic
Hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia — CHECK AND CORRECT THESE FIRST in any neonatal seizure
Inborn error of metabolism
Initially well, deteriorates day 2–3+; resembles late-onset sepsis without a clear source
Cerebral malformation
Refractory from the first days; MRI
Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy
Rare (ALDH7A1); refractory seizures responding to a pyridoxine trial
Benign familial neonatal seizures
Positive family history, self-limited, otherwise well
Always first
Correct glucose, calcium, magnesium
In parallel with — not instead of — an antiseizure drug if seizures are ongoing
1st-line
Phenobarbital: load 20 mg/kg IV (may repeat in increments to a max total load ~40 mg/kg); maintenance 3–5 mg/kg/day
Standard of care in most current protocols despite preclinical neuroapoptosis concerns
2nd-line
(Fos)phenytoin: load 20 mg PE/kg IV; maintenance 3–5 mg/kg/day
Cardiac monitoring during the load; narrow therapeutic window
Increasingly used earlier
Levetiracetam: load 20–40 mg/kg IV; maintenance 10–80 mg/kg/day
Favourable safety profile — moving earlier in some protocols; practice varies by institution
Refractory / diagnostic trial
Pyridoxine 100 mg IV single dose (with EEG monitoring if possible)
For suspected pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy or truly refractory seizures of unclear cause

buildNote: Tier 1. Doses are standard neonatal ranges. The 'check glucose/Ca/Mg first' rule is the single highest-yield bedside point.  Related: neonatal-hie-cooling, infant-of-diabetic-mother, neonatal-jaundice, peds-midazolam-status.
